Ada —

Three days out and the bunk smells of diesel and somebody else's socks, and I have decided to spend my one good hour of the evening on you, so put the kettle on before you read this.

You remember the knot in the third bench plank, the one that looks like an eye. You said it was watching us when we came in, and you turned it to face the wall with your towel like it was a nosy neighbour, and I laughed so hard I had to sit down on the hot cedar with my bare arse and yelped. That was the first thing you did to me that night: you made me laugh until I burned myself.

Then you knelt on the slatted floor between my knees, and you were not laughing anymore. You had that look you get on the water when the swell turns and you've already decided which way to go. You put your hands flat on my thighs and pushed them open, slow, and you kissed the inside of my left knee, and then higher, and higher, and you made me wait for it until I said your name like a complaint.

When you finally put your mouth on me I grabbed the edge of the bench so hard I left a splinter in my palm that I only found on the ship. You licked me open with the flat of your tongue, long and unhurried, and then you found my clit and stayed there, sucking it gently and then not gently, and you slid two fingers inside me and curled them the way you know I like, and I could hear how wet I was over the hiss of the stones. You held my hip down with your free hand when I tried to lift off the bench. I was loud. The harbourmaster's dog started barking. You did not stop.

I came with your fingers inside me and your mouth on me and my heel braced against the water bucket, and it went on long enough that I forgot the bucket and kicked it over and the steam came up around both of us like the room was breathing out.

~~I was sorry to leave you that night.~~ I was furious that I had to leave you that night, and I still am.

You climbed up into my lap afterwa— no. You climbed up into my lap while I was still shaking, and you were so wet against my thigh that I groaned, and you rocked against me, slow and greedy, your nipples hard against my mouth, while I sucked one and then the other and you held my head there by the hair. I put my hand between us and you pushed down onto my fingers and rode them, and I pressed my thumb on your clit and you swore at me in the Yoruba your grandmother taught you for exactly such occasions. You told me not to stop. I did not stop. You came with your forehead against mine and your mouth open and no sound at all, the way you do, the whole of you clenching around my fingers, and then you laughed into my neck like you'd gotten away with something.

The knot in the plank had worked its way out from behind the towel by then. It was looking right at us. You said, "Let it look," and kissed me, and I tasted myself on you.

We stayed until the stones went dull. You poured the last of the water over my head and told me I was a terrible sailor and an excellent wife, in that order, and I told you that you had it backwards.

I have the splinter in a matchbox. I am not sentimental. I am keeping it as evidence.

Here is what I am trying to say. On the second night out, in the dark, I lay in this bunk and thought of that knot in the cedar, the eye you turned to the wall, and I understood that it was me, all along: me watching you, me unable to look away, me wanting to be turned to face the wall so I wouldn't have to see the ship leave. You turned it back. Of course you did.

Kiss the dog. Don't let anyone else sit on the third plank.

M.
